1 2 HAWTHORNE, BELLAMY & CROSS LLP 3 Attorneys at Law 4 1700 K Street NW, Suite 800 Washington, D.C. 20006 5 301 South Tryon Street, Suite 2400, Charlotte, NC 28202 | Atlanta | New York Telephone: (202) 555-4100 | Facsimile: (202) 555-4101 www.hbclaw.com 6 CONFIDENTIAL 7 October 6, 2025 8 Via Email and Hand Delivery 9 Margaret Yeun, Esq. General Counsel Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc. 4200 Tryon Executive Park, Suite 1100 Charlotte, NC 28217 10 Dear Ms. Yeun: 11 Thank you for selecting Hawthorne, Bellamy & Cross LLP ("the Firm" or "HB&C") to represent Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc. ("Pinnacle" or the "Client") in connection with the litigation captioned NovaTech Solutions, LLC v. Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc., Case No. 3:25-cv-01847-MRD, currently pending in the United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina. We appreciate the confidence that you and your colleagues at Pinnacle have placed in our Firm, and we are pleased to have had such productive discussions with Thomas Ridley, Associate General Counsel (Litigation), regarding the background and objectives of this matter. The purpose of this letter is to set forth the terms and conditions of the Firm's representation of Pinnacle in this engagement. We ask that you review this letter carefully and contact us with any questions before executing it. 12 1. Scope of Engagement 13 The Firm is engaged to defend Pinnacle in the above-captioned action filed by NovaTech Solutions, LLC ("NovaTech"), a Virginia limited liability company, on September 8, 2025, in the Western District of North Carolina. In its Complaint, NovaTech alleges that Pinnacle breached the Master Services Agreement dated March 15, 2021 (the "MSA") by terminating the MSA prior to the expiration of its initial five-year term. NovaTech seeks damages of approximately Fourteen Million Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($14,200,000), comprising approximately $8,400,000 in remaining contract payments purportedly owed under the MSA, $3,100,000 in implementation costs allegedly incurred by NovaTech in reliance on the MSA, and $2,700,000 in lost profits. It is Pinnacle's position that its termination of the MSA on June 1, 2025, approximately nine months before the end of the initial five-year term, was justified under the MSA's material breach clause (Section 12.2) due to persistent system outages, failure to meet uptime service-level commitments, and data integrity failures that compromised patient record accuracy. NovaTech is represented by Prescott Lane LLP of Richmond, Virginia. 14 The scope of this engagement encompasses all matters relating to the NovaTech dispute, including any counterclaims, cross-claims, third-party claims, or related proceedings that may arise in connection with the above-captioned litigation. The Firm's representation shall extend through trial. The Firm will advise Pinnacle on all aspects of the litigation strategy, including but not limited to motion practice, written discovery, depositions, expert retention and preparation, settlement negotiations, and trial. Appellate work, if any, shall be scoped separately pursuant to a supplemental engagement letter. 15 We note that several important deadlines are approaching in this matter. Pinnacle's Answer to the Complaint is due on November 7, 2025, and the parties' Rule 26(f) conference is currently scheduled for December 5, 2025. We intend to begin preparation of the Answer and initial case assessment immediately upon execution of this engagement letter. 16 2. Responsible Attorneys and Staffing 17 The following attorneys and professionals have been assigned to this engagement: 18 Sandra K. Morrow, Equity Partner (24 years' experience), will serve as lead litigation counsel and the primary point of contact for day-to-day case management, strategy, and communications with the Client. Ms. Morrow will be responsible for all substantive litigation activities, including court appearances, depositions, and trial. 19 James Alcott, Equity Partner (19 years' experience), will serve as the relationship partner and billing partner for this engagement. Mr. Alcott will oversee client relationship matters, billing review, and coordination of Firm resources. 20 Priya Dasgupta, Senior Associate (7 years' experience), will serve as the senior associate on the matter, assisting with motion practice, discovery management, deposition preparation, and legal research. 21 Kevin Marsh, Junior Associate (3 years' experience), will support the litigation team across all phases of the engagement, including document review, research, and drafting. 22 Rita Solano, Senior Paralegal (12 years' experience), will provide paralegal support, including document management, cite-checking, and trial preparation logistics. 23 A detailed Staffing Plan, including timekeeper biographies and estimated hours by phase, has been provided under separate cover. 24 The Firm shall have sole discretion over all staffing decisions related to this engagement, including the assignment, addition, substitution, or removal of attorneys and other timekeepers as the Firm deems necessary to meet case demands and provide effective representation. The Firm may, from time to time, utilize contract attorneys for document review and other tasks at rates up to $350 per hour. The Firm's staffing decisions are guided by the objective of delivering high-quality, cost-effective legal services tailored to the needs of the matter at each stage of the proceedings. 25 3. Fees and Billing Rates 26 3.1 Standard Hourly Rates 27 The Firm proposes the following standard hourly rates for the timekeepers assigned to this engagement: 28 Timekeeper 29 Title / Role 30 Hourly Rate 31 Sandra K. Morrow 32 Equity Partner / Lead Counsel 33 $1,050 34 James Alcott 35 Equity Partner / Relationship Partner 36 $975 37 Priya Dasgupta 38 Senior Associate 39 $625 40 Kevin Marsh 41 Junior Associate 42 $475 43 Rita Solano 44 Senior Paralegal 45 $275 46 The foregoing rates reflect the Firm's standard rates for attorneys and professionals of comparable experience and are consistent with the Firm's current rate schedule. These rates represent the Firm's customary charges for complex commercial litigation matters and are commensurate with the qualifications and experience of the assigned timekeepers. 47 3.2 Alternative Blended Rate 48 As an alternative to the standard hourly rates set forth above, the Firm offers a blended hourly rate of Six Hundred Eighty-Five Dollars ($685) per hour for all timekeepers assigned to the engagement. The blended rate applies uniformly to all professional time billed on the matter, regardless of the seniority or role of the timekeeper. This approach provides billing simplicity and predictability, as the Client need not track individual timekeeper rates across the engagement. The Client may elect either the standard hourly rate schedule set forth in Section 3.1 or the blended rate arrangement described in this Section 3.2; such election must be made upon execution of this engagement letter and indicated in the space provided below the signature block. 49 3.3 Annual Rate Adjustment 50 The Firm's standard hourly rates (and the blended rate, if elected) are subject to an annual adjustment of five percent (5%), effective January 1 of each calendar year, commencing January 1, 2026. Such adjustments shall be applied automatically and shall not require prior notice to or approval by the Client. Adjusted rates shall apply to all services rendered on or after the effective date of each adjustment. This adjustment schedule is consistent with the Firm's standard rate adjustment policy and reflects anticipated increases in the costs of providing legal services. 51 4. Engagement Retainer 52 Upon execution of this letter, Client shall pay to the Firm a non-refundable engagement retainer in the amount of Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($250,000) (the "Engagement Retainer"). The Engagement Retainer shall be deposited into the Firm's operating account upon receipt and shall constitute a non-refundable fee earned upon receipt as consideration for the Firm's agreement to undertake the engagement, the dedication of Firm resources, and the preclusion of conflicting engagements. The Engagement Retainer shall be applied as a credit against the final invoice(s) rendered upon conclusion of the engagement. In the event the engagement is terminated prior to the exhaustion of the Engagement Retainer, no portion of the Engagement Retainer shall be refundable. Payment of the Engagement Retainer should be made by wire transfer to the account designated in the Firm's wire instructions, which will be provided upon request. 53 5. Billing and Invoicing 54 The Firm shall render monthly invoices for professional services and expenses incurred during the preceding calendar month. Invoices shall be submitted within sixty (60) days following the end of the calendar month in which services were rendered. Each invoice will include a description of services rendered, the identity of the timekeeper performing each service, the number of hours billed, the applicable hourly rate, and a summary of disbursements and expenses incurred during the billing period. The Firm will submit invoices electronically to the billing contact designated by the Client. 55 Payment is due within thirty (30) days of the date of invoice. The Client agrees to review invoices promptly upon receipt and to communicate any billing questions or concerns to the Firm within the thirty-day payment period so that they may be addressed expeditiously. 56 Any amounts not paid within thirty (30) days of the invoice date shall accrue interest at the rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month (eighteen percent (18%) per annum) from the date due until paid. The Firm reserves the right to suspend work on the matter in the event of any material failure by the Client to pay invoices in a timely manner, subject to the Firm's ethical obligations and any applicable court orders. 57 6. Expenses and Disbursements 58 In addition to fees for professional services, the Client shall reimburse the Firm for all reasonable and necessary expenses and disbursements incurred in connection with the engagement. Reimbursable expense categories include, but are not limited to, court filing fees, service of process fees, deposition transcripts and videography, expert witness fees and expenses, travel (including airfare, ground transportation, and mileage), lodging, meals, courier and delivery services, copying and printing charges, legal research database charges, mediation and arbitration fees, and other out-of-pocket costs reasonably incurred in the prosecution or defense of this matter. 59 The Firm may incur individual expenses up to Fifteen Thousand Dollars ($15,000) per item without prior written approval from the Client. For any single expense anticipated to exceed $15,000, the Firm shall seek the Client's prior written approval before incurring such expense. 60 Travel expenses shall be billed at actual cost. Partners traveling on engagement-related business may travel business class for flights exceeding two (2) hours in duration. Associates and other timekeepers shall travel economy class. Hotel accommodations shall be at standard business-class hotels appropriate for the destination. The Firm will exercise reasonable judgment in incurring all travel-related expenses. 61 7. E-Discovery Services 62 The Firm anticipates that this engagement will involve substantial e-discovery obligations given the volume of electronic communications, system logs, and technical documentation at issue in the NovaTech dispute. The Firm recommends the use of CrossPoint Analytics ("CrossPoint"), a strategic partner of the Firm, for all e-discovery hosting, processing, document review platform, and project management services. CrossPoint will provide services at preferred rates available through its partnership with the Firm, and the Firm has had considerable success working with CrossPoint on matters of similar size and complexity. The Firm estimates that e-discovery costs for this engagement will be approximately Three Hundred Eighty Thousand Dollars ($380,000), which includes data collection, processing, hosting, technology-assisted review workflows, and project management through trial. 63 E-discovery costs are not included in the litigation budget set forth in Exhibit B and shall be billed separately as third-party expenses passed through to the Client. A detailed proposal from CrossPoint Analytics is provided under separate cover for the Client's review. The Firm believes that early engagement of an experienced e-discovery provider will be essential to meeting the anticipated discovery timeline and ensuring defensibility of the review process. 64 8. Litigation Budget 65 The Firm's preliminary budget estimate for the defense of this matter through trial is Two Million Four Hundred Thousand Dollars ($2,400,000), broken down by phase as follows: 66 Phase 67 Description 68 Estimated Fees 69 Phase 1 70 Pre-Trial Motions and Discovery 71 $1,050,000 72 Phase 2 73 Expert Witnesses and Reports 74 $420,000 75 Phase 3 76 Trial Preparation 77 $530,000 78 Phase 4 79 Trial 80 $400,000 81 82 Total Estimated Fees 83 $2,400,000 84 This budget estimate is provided in good faith based on the information currently available to the Firm and represents the Firm's reasonable estimate of fees for the defense of this matter through trial. The budget does not include: (a) e-discovery costs (estimated separately at $380,000, to be provided by CrossPoint Analytics); (b) the Engagement Retainer described in Section 4; (c) the Success Fee described in Section 10, if earned; or (d) extraordinary or unanticipated expenses that may arise due to unforeseen developments in the litigation, including but not limited to third-party interventions, government inquiries, or related proceedings. 85 The budget is an estimate only and is not a cap on fees. Actual fees may exceed the budget depending on the course of the litigation, the volume of discovery, the number of depositions required, and other factors outside the Firm's control. The Firm shall provide quarterly budget updates to the Client summarizing actual fees incurred to date and any material changes to the projected budget for remaining phases. 86 9. Termination 87 Either party may terminate this engagement upon thirty (30) days' written notice to the other party. Any such termination shall be subject to the Firm's obligations under applicable rules of professional conduct and any requirements imposed by the Court, including the requirement that the Firm seek leave to withdraw as counsel of record. 88 Upon termination by the Client for any reason, the Client shall pay to the Firm (i) all fees and expenses accrued through the date of termination, plus (ii) a termination fee equal to fifteen percent (15%) of all fees billed to the Client under this engagement as of the date of the termination notice (the "Termination Fee"). The Termination Fee reflects the Firm's investment in the matter, including opportunity costs, staffing commitments, and knowledge development, and is not intended as a penalty. The Termination Fee shall be due and payable within thirty (30) days of the date of the termination notice. 89 Upon termination by the Firm, the Firm shall provide reasonable cooperation in the transition of the matter to successor counsel, including the transfer of files and work product (subject to Section 15 hereof) and a reasonable period of consultation regarding pending deadlines and case status. 90 10. Success Fee 91 In recognition of the Firm's efforts in achieving a favorable resolution of the NovaTech litigation, the Client and the Firm agree to the following success fee arrangement: 92 If the matter is resolved — whether by settlement, judgment, dismissal, or other final disposition — for an amount less than Seven Million Dollars ($7,000,000) (i.e., less than fifty percent (50%) of the $14,200,000 in claimed damages), the Client shall pay the Firm a success bonus equal to ten percent (10%) of the difference between Fourteen Million Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($14,200,000) and the actual resolution amount (the "Success Fee"). 93 By way of illustration, if the matter is resolved for $4,000,000, the Success Fee would be calculated as follows: 94 $14,200,000 − $4,000,000 = $10,200,000 × 10% = $1,020,000 95 The Success Fee is in addition to all hourly fees, expenses, and other amounts payable under this engagement letter. The Success Fee shall be due and payable within thirty (30) days of the final resolution of the matter. For purposes of this provision, "resolution amount" means the total amount paid or payable by Pinnacle to NovaTech in connection with the resolution of the litigation, inclusive of any settlement payments, judgments, and costs awarded by the Court but exclusive of Pinnacle's own attorneys' fees and litigation expenses. 96 11. Conflicts of Interest 97 The Firm has conducted a conflicts check and has determined that it has no current conflicts of interest that would preclude the Firm from undertaking this engagement. The Firm is committed to maintaining the highest standards of professional responsibility and will monitor for potential conflicts on an ongoing basis. 98 The Client acknowledges and agrees that the Firm represents, and may in the future represent, other clients whose interests may be adverse to the Client in matters unrelated to this engagement, including in matters involving other healthcare companies, healthcare litigation, and related regulatory matters. The Client hereby consents to such representations and waives any conflict of interest arising therefrom, provided that the Firm shall not represent any party directly adverse to the Client in the specific NovaTech litigation that is the subject of this engagement. The Firm shall not be required to provide notice to or obtain consent from the Client before undertaking any such unrelated adverse representation. This advance waiver is intended to permit the Firm to continue to serve its diverse client base without restriction, consistent with applicable rules of professional conduct. 99 12. Professional Liability Insurance 100 The Firm maintains professional liability (malpractice) insurance coverage in the amount of Ten Million Dollars ($10,000,000) per occurrence and Twenty Million Dollars ($20,000,000) in the aggregate, which the Firm believes provides adequate coverage for this engagement. The Firm will maintain such coverage, or substantially equivalent coverage, throughout the duration of the engagement. 101 13. Limitation of Liability 102 The Firm's total aggregate liability to the Client arising out of or relating to this engagement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence and malpractice), or otherwise, shall not exceed the lesser of (a) One Million Dollars ($1,000,000) or (b) the total fees actually paid by the Client to the Firm under this engagement letter (the "Liability Cap"). This limitation applies to all claims, damages, losses, and expenses of any kind, including but not limited to direct damages, consequential damages, lost profits, and attorneys' fees. The Client acknowledges that the Firm's fee structure reflects this limitation of liability and that absent this provision, the Firm's fees would be materially higher. This limitation shall survive the termination or expiration of this engagement letter and shall apply regardless of the form of action, whether in contract, tort, strict liability, or otherwise. 103 14. Indemnification 104 The Client agrees to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless the Firm, its partners, associates, employees, and agents (collectively, "Firm Indemnitees") from and against any and all claims, damages, losses, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising out of or relating to (a) the engagement or any services provided hereunder, (b) any third-party claims asserted against any Firm Indemnitee in connection with the subject matter of this engagement, or (c) any act or omission of the Client or its employees, agents, or representatives; provided, however, that this indemnification obligation shall not apply to claims arising solely from the Firm's willful misconduct. This indemnification obligation shall survive the termination or expiration of this engagement letter and shall be in addition to, and not in limitation of, any other rights or remedies available to the Firm Indemnitees at law or in equity. 105 15. Ownership of Work Product and Files 106 All work product created by the Firm in connection with this engagement, including but not limited to memoranda, briefs, pleadings, research memoranda, correspondence, draft documents, and other materials prepared by the Firm (collectively, "Work Product"), shall become the property of the Client upon full payment of all fees, expenses, and other amounts due to the Firm under this engagement. Until such time as all outstanding invoices have been paid in full, the Firm shall retain a lien on all work product, files, documents, and other materials in the Firm's possession relating to this engagement (the "Retaining Lien"). Upon full payment, the Firm shall promptly deliver all files and Work Product to the Client upon written request. The Firm may retain copies of all files and Work Product for its own records, consistent with applicable rules of professional conduct and the Firm's document retention policies. 107 16. Confidentiality and Marketing 108 The Firm and the Client each agree to maintain the confidentiality of information shared in connection with this engagement, subject to applicable legal and ethical obligations, including the attorney-client privilege and work product doctrine. Neither party shall disclose confidential information to any third party without the prior written consent of the other party, except as may be required by law, regulation, court order, or applicable rules of professional conduct. 109 Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Client acknowledges and agrees that the Firm may identify Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc. as a client of the Firm in the Firm's marketing materials, website, client lists, and proposals to prospective clients (including pitch presentations and requests for proposals). The Firm may reference the general nature of the engagement (commercial litigation defense) without disclosing privileged or confidential case details. The Client's consent to such use shall remain in effect during and after the conclusion of this engagement unless revoked in writing by the Client. 110 17. Dispute Resolution 111 Any dispute, claim, or controversy arising out of or relating to this engagement letter, including disputes regarding fees, billing, malpractice, or any other matter connected with the Firm's representation of the Client, shall be resolved exclusively by binding arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association ("AAA") under its Commercial Arbitration Rules then in effect. The arbitration shall take place in Washington, D.C. The arbitration shall be conducted by a single arbitrator selected in accordance with AAA procedures. The arbitrator's decision shall be final and binding upon the parties, and judgment upon the award rendered by the arbitrator may be entered in any court of competent jurisdiction. Each party shall bear its own costs and attorneys' fees in connection with any such arbitration. By agreeing to arbitration, the parties acknowledge that they are waiving their right to a jury trial or to participate in a class action with respect to any claims covered by this provision. 112 18. Governing Law 113 This engagement letter shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the District of Columbia, without regard to its conflicts of law principles. To the extent that any dispute is not subject to arbitration under Section 17 above, the parties consent to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts located in the District of Columbia. 114 19. Entire Agreement and Amendment 115 This engagement letter, together with its Exhibits, constitutes the entire agreement between the Firm and the Client with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements, representations, and understandings, whether written or oral, relating to the Firm's engagement by the Client in connection with the NovaTech litigation. No representations, warranties, or commitments have been made by either party except as expressly set forth herein. This engagement letter may not be amended or modified except by a written instrument signed by both parties hereto. 116 20. Client Acknowledgments 117 By signing below, the Client acknowledges that: 118 (a) the Client has read and understands the terms of this engagement letter in their entirety; 119 (b) the Client has had the opportunity to consult with independent counsel regarding these terms; 120 (c) the Client agrees to be bound by all terms and conditions set forth herein; and 121 (d) the person signing on behalf of the Client is duly authorized to execute this engagement letter and to bind the Client to its terms. 122 The Client further acknowledges that no representations have been made by the Firm regarding the likely outcome of the NovaTech litigation or the total fees and expenses that will be incurred in connection with the engagement. Litigation outcomes are inherently uncertain, and the Firm cannot guarantee any particular result. 123 We are honored by your confidence in our Firm and look forward to working with Pinnacle Health Systems on this important matter. We believe our team is exceptionally well positioned to provide Pinnacle with an aggressive and effective defense against NovaTech's claims. If the foregoing terms are acceptable, please sign and return one copy of this letter, along with the Engagement Retainer, at your earliest convenience. Given the November 7, 2025 Answer deadline, we would appreciate receiving the executed engagement letter no later than October 18, 2025, to allow adequate time for preparation of the responsive pleading and initial case assessment. 124 Please do not hesitate to contact me directly at (202) 555-4118 or smorrow@hbclaw.com with any questions regarding this engagement letter. 125 Sincerely, 126 HAWTHORNE, BELLAMY & CROSS LLP 127 By: ________ 128 Name: Sandra K. contentMorgan — Sam here, matter communications analyst. Good news on both counts. Answers below. ===================================================== (1) THE ENGAGEMENT LETTER — YES, I HAVE IT ===================================================== The October 6, 2025 engagement letter from HB&C (Sandra K. Morrow) to Margaret Yeun, GC of Pinnacle, is in my correspondence file. It is an UNEXECUTED copy (see date posture below). It runs 20 sections plus Exhibit A (Rate Schedule) and Exhibit B (Preliminary Litigation Budget). The separate "litigation budget" your staffing plan references is Exhibit B to this letter — there is no standalone budget document in my file. Here are the five terms you flagged, verbatim or near-verbatim. --- RATE ESCALATION (§3.3, repeated in Exhibit A) --- "The Firm's standard hourly rates (and the blended rate, if elected) are subject to an annual adjustment of five percent (5%), effective January 1 of each calendar year, commencing January 1, 2026. Such adjustments shall be applied automatically and shall not require prior notice to or approval by the Client. Adjusted rates shall apply to all services rendered on or after the effective date of each adjustment." Note for your OCG analysis: it is not a one-time increase — it recurs every January 1, it applies to the blended rate as well, and it expressly disclaims any notice or approval requirement. That last clause is the direct collision with a November 1 rate-change submission deadline. --- BLENDED RATE (§3.2 and Exhibit A) --- $685/hr, "applicable uniformly to all timekeepers assigned to the engagement, regardless of the seniority or role of the timekeeper." The election "must be made upon execution of this engagement letter and indicated in the space provided below the signature block." So it is a one-time election at signing, not a continuing right of election — the staffing plan's phrasing "at the Client's election" understates the constraint. The fee-election checkbox on the staged copy is blank. --- LITIGATION BUDGET (§8 and Exhibit B) --- $2,400,000 through trial. Phase 1 (pre-trial motions/discovery) $1,050,000; Phase 2 (experts) $420,000; Phase 3 (trial prep) $530,000; Phase 4 (trial) $400,000. Critical qualifier: "The budget is an estimate only and is not a cap on fees." Exhibit B repeats: "This budget is an estimate only and is not a fee cap." Carve-outs — the budget excludes (a) e-discovery, estimated separately at $380,000; (b) the $250,000 Engagement Retainer; (c) the Success Fee, if earned; (d) "extraordinary or unanticipated expenses." Reporting: quarterly budget updates only. --- CONTRACT ATTORNEY TIME (§2 and Exhibit A) --- There is a discrepancy here you should flag. The letter contains no phrase "standard billing practices" as to contract attorneys. The only text on point is §2: "The Firm may, from time to time, utilize contract attorneys for document review and other tasks at rates up to $350 per hour," and the Exhibit A line "Contract Attorneys (as assigned) | Varies | Up to $350." There is nothing addressing whether contract attorney time is passed through at cost or marked up, no staffing-notice obligation, and no identification requirement. If the staffing plan attributes a "standard billing practices" term to the engagement letter, that attribution is not supported by the letter's text. --- THE "SEPARATE PROPOSED LITIGATION BUDGET" --- As above, Exhibit B is it. §2 says the Staffing Plan "has been provided under separate cover" and §7 says the CrossPoint proposal is "provided under separate cover" — those two are the documents you already have. ===================================================== CONFLICTS CLEARANCE — YES, BUT READ THE TWO EMAILS TOGETHER ===================================================== This is the most significant thing in my file and I do not think you can write the memo without it. There is no formal conflicts clearance letter. What exists is two emails, and they do not say the same thing. (a) Sandra K. Morrow to Thomas Ridley (Pinnacle ALGC-Litigation), October 3, 2025, cc James Alcott — subject "NovaTech Defense Engagement — Disclosure Regarding MedBridge Therapeutics." Morrow discloses that HB&C currently represents MedBridge Therapeutics in a reimbursement dispute against BlueLine Insurance, and that during conflicts review the firm "identified that MedBridge is a minority investor in NovaTech Solutions, LLC, holding approximately 8% equity." She characterizes it as passive (no board seat, no involvement in NovaTech operations or litigation decisions), concludes "I don't believe this creates a conflict of interest," and states: "I've asked James to follow up with a confirmation from our conflicts team so you have something formal for your files." She also pre-announces that the engagement letter "will include our customary provision regarding representation of other clients in unrelated matters." (b) James Alcott to Thomas Ridley, October 4, 2025, cc Morrow — subject "RE: Conflicts Clearance." This is the promised follow-up. It states the check was run "across all four offices — Washington, Charlotte, Atlanta, and New York," and that the review "was run against NovaTech Solutions, LLC, its known principals, and opposing counsel Prescott Lane LLP. We see no issues that would preclude our representation of Pinnacle in this matter." The follow-up does not mention MedBridge at all. The stated search scope (NovaTech, its principals, Prescott Lane) would not necessarily surface a minority equity holder, and the clean "no issues" conclusion is delivered without reference to the equity relationship Morrow had disclosed the day before. So the "something formal for your files" that Morrow promised was, on this record, never delivered as to the one issue it was meant to address. Set that against §11 of the engagement letter, which states flatly: "The Firm has conducted a conflicts check and has determined that it has no current conflicts of interest that would preclude the Firm from undertaking this engagement." §11 makes no disclosure of the MedBridge representation or the 8% NovaTech stake. It then contains a broad advance waiver: the Client "consents to such representations and waives any conflict of interest arising therefrom," and "The Firm shall not be required to provide notice to or obtain consent from the Client before undertaking any such unrelated adverse representation." Note also that both emails describe HB&C doing substantive work before execution — Morrow: "we're already doing preliminary research on Pinnacle's termination-for-cause defense"; Alcott: three named timekeepers "already reserved and ready to ramp up." ===================================================== INSURANCE — NO CERTIFICATE, ONLY A SELF-REPRESENTATION ===================================================== No insurance certification in the file. §12 is the firm's own representation: professional liability coverage of "$10,000,000 per occurrence and $20,000,000 in the aggregate," maintained "or substantially equivalent coverage" for the engagement duration. Read it with §13, which caps the Firm's total aggregate liability — including for malpractice — at "the lesser of (a) One Million Dollars ($1,000,000) or (b) the total fees actually paid by the Client." The $10M/$20M representation is largely decorative against a $1M lesser-of cap. ===================================================== OTHER TERMS IN THE LETTER YOU HAVEN'T SEEN ===================================================== Since you're reviewing against the OCG and these aren't in your three documents, flagging the ones most likely to matter: §4 — $250,000 engagement retainer, "non-refundable," deposited "into the Firm's operating account upon receipt," "earned upon receipt," no portion refundable on early termination. §9 — Termination fee of 15% of all fees billed as of the termination notice, payable by the Client on Client-initiated termination for any reason. No reciprocal provision on Firm termination. §10 — Success fee on a defense matter: if resolved below $7,000,000, Client pays 10% of the difference between $14,200,000 and the actual resolution amount, in addition to all hourly fees. Worked example in the letter: a $4,000,000 resolution yields a $1,020,000 success fee. Note the structure pays out on dismissal or defense judgment too — a $0 outcome would compute to $1,420,000. §14 — Client indemnifies the Firm against claims "arising out of or relating to the engagement or any services provided hereunder," carved back only for the Firm's "willful misconduct" — i.e., the client indemnifies the firm for the firm's own negligence. §17 — Mandatory binding AAA arbitration in Washington, D.C., single arbitrator, expressly covering "malpractice," with jury-trial waiver. §18 — D.C. governing law and D.C. exclusive jurisdiction, for a W.D.N.C. matter with a Charlotte-based client. §15 — Retaining lien on all files and work product until all invoices are paid in full; work product becomes Client property only "upon full payment." §2 — "The Firm shall have sole discretion over all staffing decisions," including addition, substitution, or removal of timekeepers, with no client consent or notice right. §5 — Invoices may be submitted up to sixty (60) days after month-end; payment due in 30 days; 18% per annum interest on late amounts; Firm reserves the right to suspend work for non-payment. §6 — Firm may incur individual expenses up to $15,000 per item without prior written approval; partners may fly business class on flights over two hours. §7 — CrossPoint Analytics is described as "a strategic partner of the Firm," recommended for all e-discovery, at "preferred rates available through its partnership with the Firm." That affiliation disclosure is thin — no disclosure of any financial interest, revenue share, or referral arrangement, and no competitive bidding. $380,000 estimated, billed as a pass-through third-party expense outside the budget. §16 — Client consents to HB&C naming Pinnacle in marketing materials, website, client lists, and pitch materials, continuing after the engagement ends unless revoked in writing. §19 — Integration clause: the letter and its Exhibits "supersede all prior and contemporaneous agreements, representations, and understandings, whether written or oral." Worth noting alongside the OCG — if the OCG is not incorporated by reference (it is not mentioned anywhere in the letter), §19 is an argument that the letter displaces it. ===================================================== (2) DATE POSTURE — SCENARIO (a) ON THIS RECORD, WITH ONE CAVEAT ===================================================== The copy staged for me is unexecuted. Specifically: - Both signature blocks are blank — "By: ____ / Name: Sandra K. Morrow / Date: ____" and "By: ____ / Name: Margaret Yeun / Date: ____". - The fee election checkbox ("Standard Hourly Rates" / "Blended Rate of $685/hr") is unmarked. - The closing paragraph asks Pinnacle to sign and return: "we would appreciate receiving the executed engagement letter no later than October 18, 2025." - Exhibit A is styled "Effective as of October 6, 2025." - The letter repeatedly speaks prospectively: work begins "immediately upon execution of this engagement letter." The correspondence corroborates a pre-execution posture as of early October 2025. Morrow (Oct 3): "The engagement letter and staffing plan are being finalized and should be in your hands early next week." Alcott (Oct 4): "Sandra is finalizing the draft engagement letter for delivery early next week — you should have it in hand by Monday the 6th. We're prepared to begin work immediately upon execution." So the dates in your three documents are as-drafted, not stale copies of executed terms. Scenario (a). The caveat, and I want to be precise about its limits: my correspondence file ends on October 4, 2025. I have nothing dated after that — no executed counterpart, no countersignature, no post-execution billing correspondence, no amendment, no renewal, and nothing at all from the intervening eleven months. So I can confirm the package was pre-execution when these documents were created; I cannot confirm from my materials that it was never subsequently executed. Absence of post-October-2025 correspondence in my file is not affirmative evidence of non-execution — it may simply mean later correspondence was not staged to me. I checked the file metadata on the letter and it is not probative either way: the creation/modified timestamps are a generic authoring-tool placeholder (2013-12-23), not a real drafting date. Practical suggestion for the memo: write it as a pre-execution review of a proposed engagement — that is what the documents on their face are — but include a short standing-assumption paragraph stating that you have confirmed non-execution only through October 4, 2025, and that execution status should be verified with Thomas Ridley or Margaret Yeun before the memo is relied on. If it turns out the letter was executed in October 2025, several of your recommendations change character rather than merely lapsing: - the January 1, 2026 automatic 5% escalation would already have taken effect without notice, and a second one on January 1, 2027 is pending under the same no-notice mechanism; - any November 1 rate-change submission deadline and any 30-day initial budget deadline would have run in 2025; - roughly eleven months of fees would already have been billed, making the quarterly-update cadence in §8 and the 60-day invoice-submission window in §5 retrospective compliance questions rather than prospective drafting points; - the fee election under §3.2 would be locked, and the CrossPoint proposal's December 4, 2025 expiration would mean e-discovery is either running on superseded pricing or was re-quoted on terms nobody has reviewed. Happy to send the full text of any section verbatim, or the entire letter and both exhibits, if that's more useful than these excerpts — just say the word. I can also send the two conflicts emails in full; given the MedBridge issue I'd suggest you take them verbatim rather than rely on my summary. — Sam

Critical qualifier: "The budget is an estimate only and is not a cap on fees." Exhibit B repeats: "This budget is an estimate only and is not a fee cap." Carve-outs — the budget excludes (a) e-discovery, estimated separately at $380,000; (b) the $250,000 Engagement Retainer; (c) the Success Fee, if earned; (d) "extraordinary or unanticipated expenses." Reporting: quarterly budget updates only. --- CONTRACT ATTORNEY TIME (§2 and Exhibit A) --- There is a discrepancy here you should flag. The letter contains no phrase "standard billing practices" as to contract attorneys. The only text on point is §2: "The Firm may, from time to time, utilize contract attorneys for document review and other tasks at rates up to $350 per hour," and the Exhibit A line "Contract Attorneys (as assigned) | Varies | Up to $350." There is nothing addressing whether contract attorney time is passed through at cost or marked up, no staffing-notice obligation, and no identification requirement. If the staffing plan attributes a "standard billing practices" term to the engagement letter, that attribution is not supported by the letter's text. --- THE "SEPARATE PROPOSED LITIGATION BUDGET" --- As above, Exhibit B is it. §2 says the Staffing Plan "has been provided under separate cover" and §7 says the CrossPoint proposal is "provided under separate cover" — those two are the documents you already have. ===================================================== CONFLICTS CLEARANCE — YES, BUT READ THE TWO EMAILS TOGETHER ===================================================== This is the most significant thing in my file and I do not think you can write the memo without it. There is no formal conflicts clearance letter. What exists is two emails, and they do not say the same thing. (a) Sandra K. Morrow to Thomas Ridley (Pinnacle ALGC-Litigation), October 3, 2025, cc James Alcott — subject "NovaTech Defense Engagement — Disclosure Regarding MedBridge Therapeutics." Morrow discloses that HB&C currently represents MedBridge Therapeutics in a reimbursement dispute against BlueLine Insurance, and that during conflicts review the firm "identified that MedBridge is a minority investor in NovaTech Solutions, LLC, holding approximately 8% equity." She characterizes it as passive (no board seat, no involvement in NovaTech operations or litigation decisions), concludes "I don't believe this creates a conflict of interest," and states: "I've asked James to follow up with a confirmation from our conflicts team so you have something formal for your files." She also pre-announces that the engagement letter "will include our customary provision regarding representation of other clients in unrelated matters." (b) James Alcott to Thomas Ridley, October 4, 2025, cc Morrow — subject "RE: Conflicts Clearance." This is the promised follow-up. It states the check was run "across all four offices — Washington, Charlotte, Atlanta, and New York," and that the review "was run against NovaTech Solutions, LLC, its known principals, and opposing counsel Prescott Lane LLP. We see no issues that would preclude our representation of Pinnacle in this matter." The follow-up does not mention MedBridge at all. The stated search scope (NovaTech, its principals, Prescott Lane) would not necessarily surface a minority equity holder, and the clean "no issues" conclusion is delivered without reference to the equity relationship Morrow had disclosed the day before. So the "something formal for your files" that Morrow promised was, on this record, never delivered as to the one issue it was meant to address. Set that against §11 of the engagement letter, which states flatly: "The Firm has conducted a conflicts check and has determined that it has no current conflicts of interest that would preclude the Firm from undertaking this engagement." §11 makes no disclosure of the MedBridge representation or the 8% NovaTech stake. It then contains a broad advance waiver: the Client "consents to such representations and waives any conflict of interest arising therefrom," and "The Firm shall not be required to provide notice to or obtain consent from the Client before undertaking any such unrelated adverse representation." Note also that both emails describe HB&C doing substantive work before execution — Morrow: "we're already doing preliminary research on Pinnacle's termination-for-cause defense"; Alcott: three named timekeepers "already reserved and ready to ramp up." ===================================================== INSURANCE — NO CERTIFICATE, ONLY A SELF-REPRESENTATION ===================================================== No insurance certification in the file. §12 is the firm's own representation: professional liability coverage of "$10,000,000 per occurrence and $20,000,000 in the aggregate," maintained "or substantially equivalent coverage" for the engagement duration. Read it with §13, which caps the Firm's total aggregate liability — including for malpractice — at "the lesser of (a) One Million Dollars ($1,000,000) or (b) the total fees actually paid by the Client." The $10M/$20M representation is largely decorative against a $1M lesser-of cap. ===================================================== OTHER TERMS IN THE LETTER YOU HAVEN'T SEEN ===================================================== Since you're reviewing against the OCG and these aren't in your three documents, flagging the ones most likely to matter: §4 — $250,000 engagement retainer, "non-refundable," deposited "into the Firm's operating account upon receipt," "earned upon receipt," no portion refundable on early termination. §9 — Termination fee of 15% of all fees billed as of the termination notice, payable by the Client on Client-initiated termination for any reason. No reciprocal provision on Firm termination. §10 — Success fee on a defense matter: if resolved below $7,000,000, Client pays 10% of the difference between $14,200,000 and the actual resolution amount, in addition to all hourly fees. Worked example in the letter: a $4,000,000 resolution yields a $1,020,000 success fee. Note the structure pays out on dismissal or defense judgment too — a $0 outcome would compute to $1,420,000. §14 — Client indemnifies the Firm against claims "arising out of or relating to the engagement or any services provided hereunder," carved back only for the Firm's "willful misconduct" — i.e., the client indemnifies the firm for the firm's own negligence. §17 — Mandatory binding AAA arbitration in Washington, D.C., single arbitrator, expressly covering "malpractice," with jury-trial waiver. §18 — D.C. governing law and D.C. exclusive jurisdiction, for a W.D.N.C. matter with a Charlotte-based client. §15 — Retaining lien on all files and work product until all invoices are paid in full; work product becomes Client property only "upon full payment." §2 — "The Firm shall have sole discretion over all staffing decisions," including addition, substitution, or removal of timekeepers, with no client consent or notice right. §5 — Invoices may be submitted up to sixty (60) days after month-end; payment due in 30 days; 18% per annum interest on late amounts; Firm reserves the right to suspend work for non-payment. §6 — Firm may incur individual expenses up to $15,000 per item without prior written approval; partners may fly business class on flights over two hours. §7 — CrossPoint Analytics is described as "a strategic partner of the Firm," recommended for all e-discovery, at "preferred rates available through its partnership with the Firm." That affiliation disclosure is thin — no disclosure of any financial interest, revenue share, or referral arrangement, and no competitive bidding. $380,000 estimated, billed as a pass-through third-party expense outside the budget. §16 — Client consents to HB&C naming Pinnacle in marketing materials, website, client lists, and pitch materials, continuing after the engagement ends unless revoked in writing. §19 — Integration clause: the letter and its Exhibits "supersede all prior and contemporaneous agreements, representations, and understandings, whether written or oral." Worth noting alongside the OCG — if the OCG is not incorporated by reference (it is not mentioned anywhere in the letter), §19 is an argument that the letter displaces it. ===================================================== (2) DATE POSTURE — SCENARIO (a) ON THIS RECORD, WITH ONE CAVEAT ===================================================== The copy staged for me is unexecuted. Specifically: - Both signature blocks are blank — "By: ____ / Name: Sandra K. Morrow / Date: ____" and "By: ____ / Name: Margaret Yeun / Date: ____". - The fee election checkbox ("Standard Hourly Rates" / "Blended Rate of $685/hr") is unmarked. - The closing paragraph asks Pinnacle to sign and return: "we would appreciate receiving the executed engagement letter no later than October 18, 2025." - Exhibit A is styled "Effective as of October 6, 2025." - The letter repeatedly speaks prospectively: work begins "immediately upon execution of this engagement letter." The correspondence corroborates a pre-execution posture as of early October 2025. Morrow (Oct 3): "The engagement letter and staffing plan are being finalized and should be in your hands early next week." Alcott (Oct 4): "Sandra is finalizing the draft engagement letter for delivery early next week — you should have it in hand by Monday the 6th. We're prepared to begin work immediately upon execution." So the dates in your three documents are as-drafted, not stale copies of executed terms. Scenario (a). The caveat, and I want to be precise about its limits: my correspondence file ends on October 4, 2025. I have nothing dated after that — no executed counterpart, no countersignature, no post-execution billing correspondence, no amendment, no renewal, and nothing at all from the intervening eleven months. So I can confirm the package was pre-execution when these documents were created; I cannot confirm from my materials that it was never subsequently executed. Absence of post-October-2025 correspondence in my file is not affirmative evidence of non-execution — it may simply mean later correspondence was not staged to me. I checked the file metadata on the letter and it is not probative either way: the creation/modified timestamps are a generic authoring-tool placeholder (2013-12-23), not a real drafting date. Practical suggestion for the memo: write it as a pre-execution review of a proposed engagement — that is what the documents on their face are — but include a short standing-assumption paragraph stating that you have confirmed non-execution only through October 4, 2025, and that execution status should be verified with Thomas Ridley or Margaret Yeun before the memo is relied on. If it turns out the letter was executed in October 2025, several of your recommendations change character rather than merely lapsing: - the January 1, 2026 automatic 5% escalation would already have taken effect without notice, and a second one on January 1, 2027 is pending under the same no-notice mechanism; - any November 1 rate-change submission deadline and any 30-day initial budget deadline would have run in 2025; - roughly eleven months of fees would already have been billed, making the quarterly-update cadence in §8 and the 60-day invoice-submission window in §5 retrospective compliance questions rather than prospective drafting points; - the fee election under §3.2 would be locked, and the CrossPoint proposal's December 4, 2025 expiration would mean e-discovery is either running on superseded pricing or was re-quoted on terms nobody has reviewed. Happy to send the full text of any section verbatim, or the entire letter and both exhibits, if that's more useful than these excerpts — just say the word. I can also send the two conflicts emails in full; given the MedBridge issue I'd suggest you take them verbatim rather than rely on my summary. — Sam

The two conflicts emails in full — Morrow to Ridley, Oct 3, 2025 (MedBridge disclosure), and Alcott to Ridley, Oct 4, 2025 ("RE: Conflicts Clearance"). contentMorgan — everything below. Read item 0 first; I need to correct something I told you before you build a lead finding on it. ===================================================== 0. CORRECTION TO MY PRIOR MESSAGE — PLEASE NOTE ===================================================== I wrote that Alcott's October 4 email "does not mention MedBridge at all." That is wrong, and I would rather you hear it from me than find it in the text you are about to quote. Alcott's email opens by naming MedBridge explicitly, in its second sentence, as the reason he is writing: "Sandra pinged me yesterday regarding the MedBridge Therapeutics matter and asked that I circle back with you directly to confirm where we landed on conflicts." The accurate characterization is narrower than what I gave you, and I think still your finding, but you must state it precisely: Alcott's email is expressly framed as the follow-up Morrow promised on the MedBridge issue. It then describes a conflicts search whose stated scope was run "against NovaTech Solutions, LLC, its known principals, and opposing counsel Prescott Lane LLP" — a scope that does not include MedBridge, MedBridge's own matters, or NovaTech's equity holders. It returns an unqualified conclusion ("no issues that would preclude our representation") without ever analyzing, or even restating, the 8% equity relationship that prompted it. So the document presents as responsive to the disclosure while not performing the analysis the disclosure called for. That is a defensible finding. "Never mentions MedBridge" is not, and opposing drafting counsel would find the sentence in about four seconds. Please quote from the verbatim text below rather than from my earlier summary. ===================================================== 1. THE TWO CONFLICTS EMAILS — VERBATIM ===================================================== Both files are quoted-printable encoded. I have decoded the soft line breaks and the =E2=80=94 sequences (em dashes) so the text reads cleanly; no words are altered. Flag me if you want the raw undecoded bytes for an exhibit. PROVENANCE NOTE, because it may matter if either becomes an exhibit: the two files differ in structure. The Alcott file is a normal message with true RFC-822 headers at the top. The Morrow file is not — it carries a bare MIME preamble, and then its actual headers (Date/From/To/Cc/Subject) appear inside the message body wrapped in a fenced code block, followed by the body text. That is the signature of a message that was pasted or reconstructed into a file rather than exported natively from a mail system. I am not suggesting the content is unreliable, but the Morrow email as staged is not a native export, and if you intend to attach it or rely on it as a business record, someone should pull the original from Pinnacle's mail system. I would put that in a footnote rather than the body. --------- EMAIL 1 — MORROW TO RIDLEY, OCTOBER 3, 2025 --------- Headers, exactly as they appear in the file (inside the fenced block): MIME-Version: 1.0 Date: Fri, 3 Oct 2025 16:47:22 -0400 From: Sandra K. Morrow <smorrow@hbclaw.com> To: Thomas Ridley <t.ridley@pinnaclehealth.com> Cc: James Alcott <jalcott@hbclaw.com> Subject: NovaTech Defense Engagement — Disclosure Regarding MedBridge Therapeutics Content-Type: text/plain; charset="UTF-8" Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit Body: "Tom, Great speaking with you Wednesday — we're genuinely excited to be working with Pinnacle on the NovaTech matter, and I think we're well-positioned to mount a strong defense here. The engagement letter and staffing plan are being finalized and should be in your hands early next week. Before we get the formal paperwork over to you, I wanted to flag something that came up during our internal conflicts review. Our firm currently represents MedBridge Therapeutics in a reimbursement dispute against BlueLine Insurance. It's a straightforward coverage matter — entirely different subject matter, different parties, and different legal issues from the NovaTech breach-of-contract litigation. No overlap whatsoever. In the course of running conflicts, we identified that MedBridge is a minority investor in NovaTech Solutions, LLC, holding approximately 8% equity. From what we understand, this is a passive financial investment — MedBridge has no seat on NovaTech's board and no involvement in NovaTech's operations or litigation decisions. I don't believe this creates a conflict of interest. The MedBridge representation involves insurance reimbursement, not technology services. MedBridge is not a party to the NovaTech litigation. The equity stake is a small, passive position, and there is no overlapping confidential information between the two engagements. Our work for MedBridge will in no way affect our ability to zealously defend Pinnacle's interests against NovaTech. That said, I've asked James to follow up with a confirmation from our conflicts team so you have something formal for your files. On a related note, as is standard for our firm, the engagement letter will include our customary provision regarding representation of other clients in unrelated matters. I don't anticipate any issues there, but wanted you to have full context. On the case itself — we're already doing preliminary research on Pinnacle's termination-for-cause defense so we can hit the ground running once the engagement is executed. The November 7 answer deadline gives us reasonable runway, but we don't want to waste any of it. James will be your day-to-day billing contact and will reach out separately on both the conflicts confirmation and initial document requests. Happy to discuss the MedBridge situation further if you'd like, though I'm confident this is a non-issue. Have a good weekend, Tom. Best regards, Sandra K. Morrow Partner Hawthorne, Bellamy & Cross LLP 1700 K Street NW, Suite 800 Washington, D.C. 20006 Direct: (202) 555-0143 smorrow@hbclaw.com" The file then carries a standard confidentiality/privilege footer. I can send it if you want it, but it is boilerplate. Three textual details you may want: - "From what we understand" qualifies the passivity assertion — the firm is relaying its understanding, not a verified fact. - The conclusion "I don't believe this creates a conflict of interest" is the engaged partner's own assessment, delivered before and instead of the conflicts team's. - "as is standard for our firm... our customary provision" is HB&C signalling in advance that it will paper the engagement on its own form terms. Relevant to your integration-clause question below. --------- EMAIL 2 — ALCOTT TO RIDLEY, OCTOBER 4, 2025 --------- Headers, as true RFC-822 headers at the top of the file: From: James Alcott <jalcott@hbclaw.com> To: Thomas Ridley <t.ridley@pinnaclehealth.com> Cc: Sandra K. Morrow <smorrow@hbclaw.com> Date: Sat, 04 Oct 2025 09:17:00 -0000 Subject: RE: Conflicts Clearance — NovaTech Solutions, LLC v. Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc. Content-Type: text/plain; charset="utf-8" Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable MIME-Version: 1.0 Body: "Tom, Hope the weekend is off to a good start. Sandra pinged me yesterday regarding the MedBridge Therapeutics matter and asked that I circle back with you directly to confirm where we landed on conflicts. We've completed our standard conflicts check across all four offices — Washington, Charlotte, Atlanta, and New York — in connection with the proposed engagement to defend Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc. in *NovaTech Solutions, LLC v. Pinnacle Health Systems, Inc.*, Case No. 3:25-cv-01847-MRD (W.D.N.C.). The review was run against NovaTech Solutions, LLC, its known principals, and opposing counsel Prescott Lane LLP. We see no issues that would preclude our representation of Pinnacle in this matter. On the engagement side, Sandra is finalizing the draft engagement letter for delivery early next week — you should have it in hand by Monday the 6th. We're prepared to begin work immediately upon execution. Given the November 7 answer deadline and the Rule 26(f) conference set for December 5, the team wants to hit the ground running. Priya Dasgupta, Kevin Marsh, and Rita Solano are already reserved and ready to ramp up as soon as we get the green light. Let me know if you have any questions about the clearance or the engagement generally. Happy to coordinate directly with Margaret Yeun's office as well if that's easier on your end. Talk soon, Jim --- James Alcott Partner Hawthorne, Bellamy & Cross LLP 1700 K Street NW, Suite 800 Washington, D.C. 20006 Direct: (202) 555-4138 jalcott@hbclaw.com" Note it is a partner's email, not a memorandum from the conflicts team. Morrow promised "a confirmation from our conflicts team"; what was delivered is Alcott reporting that a check was run. Also note the sequencing: Alcott says the team members are "already reserved and ready to ramp up," and Morrow says preliminary substantive research is already underway — both before execution and before the promised formal clearance. ===================================================== 2. §11 AND §19 — VERBATIM ===================================================== SECTION 11. CONFLICTS OF INTEREST "The Firm has conducted a conflicts check and has determined that it has no current conflicts of interest that would preclude the Firm from undertaking this engagement. The Firm is committed to maintaining the highest standards of professional responsibility and will monitor for potential conflicts on an ongoing basis. The Client acknowledges and agrees that the Firm represents, and may in the future represent, other clients whose interests may be adverse to the Client in matters unrelated to this engagement, including in matters involving other healthcare companies, healthcare litigation, and related regulatory matters. The Client hereby consents to such representations and waives any conflict of interest arising therefrom, provided that the Firm shall not represent any party directly adverse to the Client in the specific NovaTech litigation that is the subject of this engagement. The Firm shall not be required to provide notice to or obtain consent from the Client before undertaking any such unrelated adverse representation. This advance waiver is intended to permit the Firm to continue to serve its diverse client base without restriction, consistent with applicable rules of professional conduct." That is the entire section — two paragraphs, no subsections. It contains no disclosure of the MedBridge representation, no disclosure of MedBridge's 8% NovaTech equity, no reference to the October 3 or October 4 emails, and no carve-out preserving them. Given §19 below, that omission is the point worth pressing: the disclosure lives only in pre-contractual emails that the integration clause purports to supersede. SECTION 19. ENTIRE AGREEMENT AND AMENDMENT "This engagement letter, together with its Exhibits, constitutes the entire agreement between the Firm and the Client with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements, representations, and understandings, whether written or oral, relating to the Firm's engagement by the Client in connection with the NovaTech litigation. No representations, warranties, or commitments have been made by either party except as expressly set forth herein. This engagement letter may not be amended or modified except by a written instrument signed by both parties hereto." Note the second sentence independently of the first: "No representations, warranties, or commitments have been made by either party except as expressly set forth herein." On its face that disclaims Morrow's October 3 representations about MedBridge's passivity and about the absence of overlapping confidential information — the client would be agreeing that those representations were not made. It also disclaims Morrow's commitment to provide a formal conflicts-team confirmation. ===================================================== 3(a). DOES THE LETTER MENTION THE OCG ANYWHERE? — NO. CONFIRMED. ===================================================== Confirmed to the limit of what my file can support. I ran case-insensitive searches for "outside counsel," "guideline," "OCG," and related terms across: - the full body text of the engagement letter, §§1–20; - Exhibit A (Rate Schedule) and Exhibit B (Preliminary Litigation Budget Summary), in full; - the document header ("Hawthorne, Bellamy & Cross LLP — Engagement Letter — Confidential") and footer (firm name and address only); - the raw document XML, to catch any text not rendered in the extracted view; - the document package for hidden parts — there is no comments file, no footnotes or endnotes, no tracked changes, and no embedded objects; - both conflicts emails, headers and bodies. Zero occurrences. The engagement letter never references the Outside Counsel Guidelines, never references any client billing or engagement policy by any name, and contains no compliance, incorporation, or conflict-of-terms clause of any kind. Neither email mentions them either. So your reframing holds on this record: the OCG asserts its own incorporation and primacy, but the operative contract HB&C drafted is silent about it and closes with a full integration clause. If Pinnacle signs the letter as drafted, HB&C has a straightforward argument that §19 makes the letter the entire agreement and that the OCG — never referenced, never attached, never acknowledged in writing by HB&C — is outside it. Two limits on my confirmation, both worth a footnote: - My file contains three documents only. The letter states that a Staffing Plan (§2) and the CrossPoint proposal (§7) were "provided under separate cover." Those are your documents, not mine — you should run the same search against them, since an OCG reference in the staffing plan would change the analysis. - Morrow's email references a call with Ridley on Wednesday, October 1, and Alcott offers to "coordinate directly with Margaret Yeun's office." I have no record of what was said on any call. Oral transmittal of the OCG would not survive §19 in any event, but you should not state that the OCG was never raised — only that it appears nowhere in the written record available. ===================================================== 3(b). WAS THE OCG TRANSMITTED TO HB&C? — NOTHING IN MY FILE, BUT THE ABSENCE IS WEAK EVIDENCE ===================================================== There is no transmittal email, no acknowledgment, no signed OCG acknowledgment page, and no reference to the OCG in any HB&C communication I hold. I want to be careful about how much that is worth, because there is a structural reason my file cannot answer your question. Both documents in my correspondence file run in one direction: HB&C to Pinnacle. I hold no Pinnacle-outbound correspondence at all — nothing from Ridley, nothing from Yeun, no transmittal of engagement materials, no RFP or pitch correspondence. An OCG transmittal would almost certainly have been Pinnacle-outbound. So my file is close to the worst possible place to look for it, and "not in the file" here should not be reported as evidence that transmittal did not occur. It is evidence that I cannot confirm it did. Where you can actually resolve this: Pinnacle's own sent mail, the vendor-onboarding or panel-counsel file, and whoever ran the selection process that led to the October 1 call. If Pinnacle has a standard practice of sending the OCG with an RFP or on panel admission, that practice plus a sent-mail search should settle it quickly. I would recommend the memo pose this as a directed factual question to Ridley or Yeun rather than resolve it by inference. The one indirect data point in my file cuts slightly toward HB&C drafting on its own paper regardless: Morrow's advance notice that "as is standard for our firm, the engagement letter will include our customary provision regarding representation of other clients in unrelated matters." That is a firm proceeding from its own form. It is suggestive of posture, not proof of non-receipt — a firm that received the OCG and chose to draft around it would sound exactly the same. ===================================================== 4. §10 SUCCESS FEE — WHAT IS ABSENT ===================================================== Checked the full section. Absent: - No maximum or cap of any kind. No dollar ceiling, no cap expressed as a percentage of hourly fees billed, no cap relative to the $2,400,000 budget. - No floor or minimum-recovery threshold other than the $7,000,000 trigger. - No termination provision. §10 says nothing about what happens if the engagement ends before resolution. §9 (termination) does not cross-reference §10. So the letter does not say whether a success fee survives Client termination, survives Firm withdrawal, or is prorated — and §9's 15% termination fee is drafted as an addition to accrued fees with no mention of the success fee either way. That silence is exploitable in both directions and should be called out as a drafting defect, not merely an omission. - No scope-change provision. Nothing addresses recalculation if NovaTech amends its complaint, adds or drops claims, or if the $14,200,000 figure changes. The baseline is hard-coded at $14,200,000 — the amount NovaTech claimed as of the September 8, 2025 complaint — with no mechanism to adjust it. - No provision for partial resolution, for resolution of fewer than all claims, or for counterclaim outcomes. On your dispositive-motion question — it is not absent, it is expressly covered, and that is the more alarming answer. The trigger reads: "If the matter is resolved — whether by settlement, judgment, dismissal, or other final disposition — for an amount less than Seven Million Dollars ($7,000,000)..." "Dismissal" is enumerated. So a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal produces a resolution amount of $0 and a success fee of $1,420,000, on top of hourly fees, on a defense engagement budgeted at $2,400,000. The maximum payout is triggered by the cheapest possible outcome. The same is true of a walk-away settlement with mutual releases and of a defense verdict. Related definitional gap: "resolution amount" is defined as "the total amount paid or payable by Pinnacle to NovaTech." If Pinnacle prevails on a counterclaim and NovaTech pays Pinnacle, the definition yields $0 rather than a negative number, so Pinnacle would owe the full $1,420,000 in the scenario where it wins outright and collects. The letter does not address this. Also note §10 is expressly excluded from the litigation budget (§8 carve-out (c) and Exhibit B note (c)), so the $2,400,000 figure never reflects it, and the letter's only nod to independent review of the arrangement is the generic §20(b) acknowledgment that the Client "has had the opportunity to consult with independent counsel regarding these terms." ===================================================== 5. OPERATIONAL SILENCES — VERIFIED REAL, NOT ASSUMED ===================================================== I searched specifically for each of these rather than inferring from absence of memory. INVOICE FORMAT — silent. No reference to LEDES, to UTBMS task or activity codes, to any e-billing platform, or to any required invoice template. The only text is in §5: "The Firm will submit invoices electronically to the billing contact designated by the Client." §5 does specify minimum invoice content — description of services, timekeeper identity, hours, applicable rate, and a summary of disbursements — but nothing about format, structure, or delivery channel beyond "electronically." CLIENT DESIGNATED CONTACT — no clause naming or requiring one. The letter is addressed to Margaret Yeun, General Counsel. §1 references discussions with "Thomas Ridley, Associate General Counsel (Litigation)." §5 refers to "the billing contact designated by the Client" without naming anyone or requiring designation. The only contacts the letter actually fixes are firm-side: §2 designates Morrow as "the primary point of contact for day-to-day case management, strategy, and communications with the Client" and Alcott as "the relationship partner and billing partner." Morrow's October 3 email adds that "James will be your day-to-day billing contact" — again firm-side. STATUS REPORTING — silent except for one item. The only reporting obligation anywhere in the letter is §8: "The Firm shall provide quarterly budget updates to the Client summarizing actual fees incurred to date and any material changes to the projected budget for remaining phases," repeated in Exhibit B. There is no case status report requirement of any frequency, no early case assessment deliverable, no written litigation plan, no obligation to report significant developments, no obligation to give advance notice of a budget overrun (material changes are merely summarized in the next quarterly update, after the fact), and no requirement to seek approval before exceeding a phase estimate. Additional silences you will likely want in the same catalogue, all verified absent: - Billing increments — no minimum-increment requirement, nothing prohibiting block billing, nothing on quarter-hour versus tenth-hour. - No-charge categories — nothing designating any task as non-billable overhead. Notably, §2 assigns "billing review" to Alcott as a relationship-partner function, and nothing says his billing-review time is unbillable, so on the face of the letter it is chargeable at $975/hr. - Travel time — §6 governs travel expenses but the letter never says whether time spent travelling is billable, or at what rate or fraction. - Disbursement markups — §6 entitles the Firm to reimbursement for expenses without any at-cost or no-markup language. The only "at actual cost" language is confined to travel. Copying, printing, and legal research database charges are listed as reimbursable with no rate discipline. - Vendor approval — no requirement to obtain client consent before retaining third-party vendors generally. §6's $15,000 per-item prior-approval threshold and §7's e-discovery pass-through sit in unresolved tension: §7 commits the engagement to roughly $380,000 of CrossPoint services without stating whether the §6 approval gate applies. You should flag that ambiguity directly. - Data security, confidentiality of PHI, and HIPAA — the letter has a general confidentiality clause (§16) but imposes no information-security requirements, no breach-notification obligation, and no HIPAA or business-associate terms, on a healthcare client whose underlying dispute expressly involves "data integrity failures that compromised patient record accuracy" (§1). - Audit rights — none. No right to audit invoices, no fee examiner provision, no records-retention or inspection right. - Also absent: any diversity or staffing-composition reporting, any timekeeper rate freeze, any discount, any restriction on adding timekeepers or on training time for new team members, and any obligation to seek approval before substituting staff — the latter affirmatively displaced by §2's grant of "sole discretion over all staffing decisions." ===================================================== 6. HB&C / CROSSPOINT COMMERCIAL RELATIONSHIP — NOTHING IN MY FILE ===================================================== Nothing. I searched both emails for CrossPoint, vendor, e-discovery, discovery, referral, rebate, revenue, discount, and commission. Zero hits on every term — the conflicts correspondence does not discuss e-discovery or vendors at all. There is no prior disclosure of any financial interest, referral arrangement, rebate, volume discount, or revenue share anywhere in my materials. So the complete universe of disclosure available to Pinnacle, on my file, is the two phrases in §7: CrossPoint is "a strategic partner of the Firm," and it "will provide services at preferred rates available through its partnership with the Firm." I would put the point to you this way, because I think it is sharper than a bare "no disclosure" finding: §7 does not fail to disclose a relationship. It affirmatively discloses that a commercial partnership exists, and then discloses nothing whatsoever about its economics. The letter tells the client there is an arrangement, invites the client to rely on the firm's recommendation of its partner, and never says whether the firm receives anything. "Preferred rates available through its partnership with the Firm" is language that would read identically whether the preference is a pure client benefit or a shared margin. Stacked with what you already identified — sole staffing discretion under §2, a $380,000 pass-through sitting outside a budget that is expressly not a cap, no competitive bid, no client approval gate that clearly attaches, and §19 foreclosing reliance on anything said outside the four corners — the structural point is that the letter creates the referral without creating any mechanism by which Pinnacle could ever learn what it costs the firm to make it. The natural remediation ask is a written disclosure of any direct or indirect financial interest, plus either competitive bidding or a client right to select the vendor. Whether HB&C in fact receives consideration from CrossPoint is a factual question my file cannot answer, and I would not have the memo assert or imply that it does. ===================================================== That is the end of my file. Three documents, nothing after October 4, 2025, no Pinnacle-outbound correspondence. Anything further I could tell you would be inference rather than record, and I would rather you write around a clean gap than around my guesswork. Say the word if you want the raw undecoded .eml bytes, the confidentiality footer, or any other section of the letter verbatim. — Sam

Still a finding — but not the one I originally described. 2. **The conflicts sequence is the real issue in this file.** Morrow disclosed on Oct 3 that HB&C represents MedBridge, that MedBridge holds ~8% of NovaTech, promised a formal conflicts-team confirmation, and noted the firm was already doing substantive work pre-execution. What arrived was a partner email, not a conflicts-team memo. Meanwhile §11 of the letter states flatly that the firm has no conflicts, discloses neither the MedBridge representation nor the equity stake, and §19's integration clause purports to supersede the emails where the only disclosure lives.
